claim: Randall places Kay's multi-focalized technique with the richly populated Victorian novel and the thick historical novel of Dorothy Dunnett rather than with single-focalizer fantasies like Tolkien, Donaldson or Wolfe.

claim: Randall argues the shifts (1) let the reader assimilate the secondary world, (2) build knowledge of character, (3) move the story from kernel to kernel, and (4) delay the unfolding of each plot-line, all serving a rhetoric of grandeur and scope.
source: Neil Randall, 'Shifting Focalization and the Strategy of Delay: The Narrative Weaving of The Fionavar Tapestry', Canadian Literature 129 (Summer 1991), reprinted on Bright Weavings
quote: the shifts delay the unfolding of the story

verdict.trueWording: The effect ... is four-fold
verdict.note: Raw page lists all four: assimilate the world of Fionavar; 'they form our knowledge of character'; 'the constant shifting moves the novel from incident to incident, and in fact makes possible the co-ordination of important events (kernels in Barthes' terminology)'; 'the shifts delay the unfolding of the story'; closing with 'all four point as well towards a rhetorical effect of grandeur and scope.' Third effect is worded 'incident to incident' with kernels glossed in the same sentence; 'kernel to kernel' is Randall's own later phrase ('The shifts in focalization move the plot from kernel to kernel').
